name: @material-tax-reporting/local-coding-assistants
description: Guided, fail-closed local Codex CLI and OpenCode launch contracts for tax-report preparation assistance.
//: The '.' entry offers TypeScript source, and there is deliberately no 'node'
condition beside it. That absence is a decision, not an oversight, so read
this before adding one.
What breaks if Node loads this entry directly: everything. Node runs a '.ts'
file only where type stripping is enabled, and the pinned toolchain in
dependency-manifest.json is Node 22.14.0 — older than the 22.18.0 that made
stripping the default. Running the entry under a stripping-disabled Node
reproduces the exact failure a build machine would see:
ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION naming src/index.ts.
Why no compiled entry exists anyway: nothing Node executes directly imports
this package by name. The only importer is apps/desktop/src/main, which
reaches it through require() inside a bundle esbuild builds; esbuild resolves
the specifier at build time and Node never sees it. A build step nobody runs
is worse than none, so none is declared.
Adding a 'node' condition is therefore a TWO-part change that must land in one
commit, and the second part is the one that gets forgotten. Part one is a
transpile-only esbuild build writing ./dist/index.js (copy the shape of
packages/surface-kernel/scripts/build.mjs; never tsc, which type-checks and
would let a type error withhold a release). Part two is wiring that build into
every consumer that resolves the 'node' condition — which includes esbuild
itself, because platform:'node' matches 'node' exactly as Node does. Verified
with a real esbuild against a package shaped like this one: with ./dist
present the bundler inlines dist/index.js instead of the source, and with
./dist absent the desktop bundle stops resolving this package at all. ./dist
is git-ignored, so a fresh checkout never has one and the breakage would show
up only away from a warm developer machine.
Sibling modules under src/ are referenced with their real '.ts' extensions, so
a Node that does strip types loads this entry as written rather than failing
on a './types.js' that has never existed.
